videos.title: Qashqai 1.2 DIG-T engine problems (1.2 Turbo)
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.2 DIG-T engine in the Qashqai and Juke 
models is the same engine as the H5Ft or
1.2 TCe in Renault and Dacia vehicles. It was 
manufactured between 2012 and 2019. The first
years were prone to a lot of software-related 
problems and could just stall or lose power
randomly, so Renault-Nissan issued several 
software updates that surprisingly fixed the
issues. If you experience random unexplained 
problems with the early-model-year 1.2 DIG-T,
make sure you have the latest available 
software update installed in the dealership.
These engines are very economical. And even 
though the horsepower is not mind-blowing at all,
the torque is very decent, and driving the 
Qashqai powered with this engine is a lot of
fun in the city traffic. For highways, you would 
want more power, but still, it’s not that bad.
Also, this is a 4-cylinder engine, 
so there are no vibrations and
juddering that you will get in 3-cylinder 
engines of such size in many other cars.
Among the common problems, I would point out 
oil consumption. The engine will start burning
some oil from the first miles of its life, and it 
will deteriorate gradually. The reason is simple:
the piston rings are not perfect and let 
some oil leak into the combustion chamber.
Repair is super expensive, so the obvious solution 
is to put up with this and just keep an eye on
the oil level to avoid low-pressure issues.
Secondly, these engines have direct injection,
and this inevitably leads to carbon buildup on 
intake valves sooner or later. If you experience
hesitation, uneven idle, or even stalling, this 
is clearly because of the contaminated valves that
need to be cleaned. Fortunately, cleaning is not 
that expensive in a good independent repair shop.
These engines are equipped with the timing chain 
and it’s not perfect. The chain is quite thin and
will elongate significantly up to 60,000 miles, 
or 100,000 kilometers. The chain kit is not that
expensive and the labor cost may not be that 
bad. But the problem is that both camshafts
are equipped with phasers for variable valve 
timing and these phasers are very often dead
at this mileage, so it makes sense to replace 
them when you are installing the new chain. The
phasers are not cheap at all and this makes the 
chain kit replacement ridiculously expensive.
And there is one more very common problem: the 
seal of the crankcase ventilation system pipe is
somehow very unreliable and may get a crack at any 
mileage. It’s not hard or expensive to replace,
but it’s very hard to locate this problem. 
So, if you experience oil pressure anomalies,
random check engine light, or unstable 
engine work, it’s a good idea to check
this seal in the PCV system first.
Other than that, these engines are
quite good to own. They will survive about 
150,000 miles or 240,000 kilometers without
major problems. But after that oil consumption is 
usually too high and extremely expensive repairs
are needed which usually means engine replacement. 
So, it’s important to know all the weaknesses when
you own a high-mileage Qashqai or are about to 
buy a used vehicle equipped with this engine.

videos.transcript_text:
Welcome to the Autorooto Freak channel.
Greetings to all viewers, subscribers,
supporters. So, to the point, the
Renault 1.2 tce engine primarily
identified by the H5F engine code is a
1.2 L 4-cylinder turbocharged gasoline
engine that was widely used across
various Renault, DEA, Nissan, and even
some Mercedes-Benz models like the
Teton. It was a significant engine for
the Renault Nissan Alliance, aiming to
provide a balance of performance and
efficiency in a compact package.
However, it gained a reputation for
significant and welldocumented issues
leading to widespread dissatisfaction
among owners and even legal action in
some cases. Let's break down its
characteristics, history, and versions.
The 1.2TCE 2TCE
H5F
engine was introduced around 2012. It
replaced older naturally aspirated
engines and aimed to offer better
performance with lower displacement due
to turbocharging. It was produced in
various power outputs typically ranging
from 115HP
to 130HP. EG, TCE 115, TCE 120, TC125,
TCE130.
Models commonly equipped with this
engine include Renault, Cleo 4, Captor,
Megane 3, Kajger, Scenic 3, DEA, Duster,
Docker, Logi, Nissan, Juke, Pulsar, Kos
K2, MercedesBenz, Seton. It's important
to distinguish this older 1.2TCE 2TCE
H5F for cylinder from a newer 1.2TCE
HR12 engine 3-cylinder found in more
recent models like the Ostrol Espace and
new Dea Duster. The issues discussed
below primarily pertain to the older H5F
review and opinions. General sentiment
initial reviews often praise the 1.2TCE
2TCE for its smoothness and refinement.
Compared to some older naturally
aspirated units or even some diesels, it
was generally quieter and offered a more
refined power delivery. Good low-end
torque. The turbocharger provided a
decent pull from low RPMs, making it
feel spritly in city driving. Decent
performance for its size. It delivered
adequate power for most everyday driving
scenarios. However, these positive
initial impressions were often
overshadowed by the engine's long-term
reliability issues. Advantages: Compact
size allows for better packaging in
smaller vehicles. Turbocharged
performance provides good power and
torque for its displacement. Relatively
smooth operation when new and
functioning correctly. It was a refined
engine. Disadvantages and major
problems. The 1.2 2TCE
H5F
engines are notoriously known for a
series of design flaws leading to
significant problems. Excessive oil
consumption. This is the most widely
reported and severe issue. A design
flaw, particularly related to the
crankase, ventilation system, and piston
rings, led to oil entering the
combustion chamber and being burned off.
This often required owners to frequently
top up oil, sometimes leading to engine
damage if neglected. Renault later
introduced modified piston rings to
address this, but many earlier engines
were affected. Timing chain issues.
While it uses a timing chain, generally
considered maintenance-free. There are
frequent reports of timing chain stretch
and tensioner failures. This can lead to
incorrect valve timing, poor engine
performance, and in severe cases,
catastrophic engine failure, carbon
deposits. Direct injection engines are
prone to carbon buildup on intake valves
and in the combustion chamber. In the
1.2TCE,
this was exacerbated by the oil
consumption issue, leading to further
performance degradation, misfires, and
potentially burned exhaust valves.
burned exhaust valves. A direct
consequence of high oil consumption and
carbon buildup leading to poor
compression, misfires, and the need for
costly cylinder head repairs or engine
replacement. Ignition coil and spark
plug failures. While less critical than
internal engine problems, these were
also reported as recurring issues.
Engine knocking/ pre-ignition. Due to
oil in the combustion chamber and carbon
deposits, the engine could experience
knocking or pre-ignition leading to
further stress on components, faults and
breakdowns, loss of power, often due to
timing chain issues, turbocharger
problems, or excessive carbon buildup,
rough idling and misfires, symptoms of
carbon deposits, burn valves, or faulty
ignition components. Engine warning
lights commonly illuminated for various
sensor faults or engine performance
issues. Complete engine failure. Seizure
in extreme cases, particularly with
ignored oil consumption. Engines could
seize due to oil starvation or severe
internal damage. Lawsuits and
investigations. The widespread nature of
these problems led to collective
lawsuits against Rena Nissan in several
countries, forcing the manufacturers to
acknowledge the issues and provide some
recourse for affected customers. Fuel
consumption. Official figures generally
indicated good fuel economy due to the
engine's small displacement and
turbocharging. However, real world fuel
consumption can vary significantly,
especially if the engine is suffering
from the common issues. Users on forums
have reported figures ranging from 6 to
7LKM
on highways to 10 to 11LKM
in heavy city traffic. Some reports
suggest that if the engine is burning
oil, fuel efficiency can also be
negatively impacted. Timing. The Renault
1.2TCE
H5F engines use a timing chain. This
component is theoretically designed to
last the life of the engine. However, as
mentioned under disadvantages, premature
timing chain stretch and tensioner
failure are known problems with this
engine, often necessitating costly
replacement. This issue is sometimes
linked to oil quality and change
intervals. Oil oil type. Renault
generally recommended oils conforming to
their RN07000
or RN0710
specifications often with ACIA A3/B4
or ACIS C3 and viscosities like 5W30
or 5W40. Crucial recommendation for this
engine due to the known oil consumption
issues is highly recommended to check
oil levels very frequently, far more
often than typical recommendations,
possibly every 1,000 to 2,000 km. Use
high quality synthetic oil, adhering
strictly to manufacturer specifications,
or even using a slightly more robust
oil, eg higher HDHS viscosity if
recommended for the climate. Reduce oil
change intervals. Many specialists and
affected owners advise changing the oil
much more frequently than the
manufacturers suggested 20,000 km or
30,000 km, often recommending every
10,000 km or annually. Consider engine
flush treatments before oil changes to
help remove sludge and carbon deposits.
In summary, the Renault 1.2TCE 2TCE H5F
engine, while offering decent
performance and refinement when new, has
a documented history of significant
reliability issues, primarily related to
excessive oil consumption, timing chain
problems, and carbon buildup, which can
lead to costly repairs, or even engine
replacement. Prospective buyers of used
vehicles with this engine should
exercise extreme caution. Ensure a full
service history is available and ideally
have a thorough pre-purchase inspection
that specifically checks for these known
problems. Regular and diligent oil
checks and more frequent oil changes
than factory recommendations are
critical for owners of these engines.
The newer 1.2TCE 2TCE HR12 3-cylinder
engine is a different design and does
not carry the same problematic
reputation as the older H5F. Thank you
for watching the video and I invite you
to subscribe to the Automotoreak
channel. Greetings to everyone and see
you in the next episode. See you soon.

hey everyone Brian your honest mechanic 
today we're tackling a crucial issue that
could be destroying your turbo engine without 
you even knowing it with over 20 years in the
business I've seen too many engines suffer from 
avoidable mistakes stick around to learn how to
protect your turbo and if you find this helpful 
please don't forget to press that like button
and subscribe all right let's get to the 
five things that damages turbo engines one
cold starts and immediate acceleration one of 
the most common mistakes I see and it's a big
one is the cold start Ando syndrome you know 
the drill it's a frosty morning you're running
late so you start your engine and immediately hit 
the gas sound familiar well I hate to break it to
you but this is one of the most damaging things 
you can do to your turbo engine why you ask when
you start a cold engine especially in freezing 
conditions the oil is as thick as molasses your
turbocharger which by the way can spin at speeds 
exceeding 200,000 revolutions per minute needs
proper lubrication ASAP accelerating hard before 
the oil has a chance to warm up that's a recipe
for disaster so what's the solution simple allow 
your engine to idle for 2 to 5 minutes before
driving it's just a few minutes of your time 
but it can add years to your engine's life two
lowquality fuel now let's talk about what you're 
putting in your tank the quality of fuel you use
it matters a lot turbochargers increase pressure 
in the combustion chamber which means your fuel
needs to withstand higher compression with without 
pre- igniting using lowquality or incorrect octane
fuel can lead to engine knocking or pre-ignition 
and trust me those little explosions in your
cylinders they're bad news for your engine always 
and I mean always refer to your vehicles owners's
manual for the recommended fuel grade if it says 
premium don't cheap out the few extra bucks at
the pump they're nothing compared to the cost of 
major engine repairs three overreliance on stop
start systems now let's talk talk about a feature 
in many modern turbocharged Vehicles stop start
systems they're great for fuel efficiency and 
Emissions but and it's a big butt they can be
trouble for turbo engines if you rely on them too 
heavily why it all comes down to oil circulation
every time the engine stops even for a few seconds 
oil flow ceases this can be a real problem if the
engine shuts off when the turbocharger is still 
hot over time this start Stop Cycle can lead to
increased wear oil cing and even damage to your 
starter motor and battery so what's the solution
use these systems wisely consider disabling 
the stop start system every once in a while
and always use highquality oil approved for 
stop start systems four immediate shutdown
after high-s speeed or high lad driving picture 
this scenario you've just finished a long Highway
Drive pull into your driveway and immediately 
shut off the engine sounds harmless right wrong
after high-speed or high load driving your 
turbocharger can reach temperatures over 1
1,000° F that's hotter than a pizza oven turning 
off the engine immediately cuts off the oil supply
leaving all that heat with nowhere to go the 
result oil cing where Oil essentially bakes
onto your turbochargers components not good the 
fix is simple let your engine idle for 30 seconds
to a minute after high stress driving before 
shutting it off it's a small step that can make
a big difference in your turbocharger lifespan 
five neglecting regular oil changes listen up
because this is crucial regular oil changes are 
the lifeblood of your turbo engine in a turbo
engine oil doesn't just lubricate it also helps 
cool the turbocharger and let me tell you that oil
degrades fast under those conditions skipping oil 
changes you might as well be throwing sand in your
engine so what should you do consider changing 
engine oil every 3,500 to 5,000 Mi and always use
high quality synthetic oil specifically formulated 
for turbocharged engines your turbo will thank you

videos.title: Renault 1.3 TCe engine: Common problems and faults
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.3 TCe engine was developed in 2017-2018, 
and it wasn’t just the Renault engine. It was
engineered by Renault-Nissan and Mercedes, 
and it has been used in a bunch of Mercedes,
Nissan, Renault, and Dacia vehicles. Actually, 
it’s a very reliable engine compared to other
downsized motors available on the market. And 
owners usually write good reviews about it.
In this video, I will focus on the problems 
and faults that you may experience with
this engine in Renault cars, but I should 
say that this is one of the best gasoline
engines made by Renault within the last decade.
First of all, it’s the 4-cylinder engine with a
good and reliable Garrett turbocharger. 
It has a very reliable timing chain,
which is quite unusual for modern engines. 
The chain can last about 250,000 kilometers,
and then it should be replaced along with 
the phasers, which is not that cheap,
but still, the lifespan is impressive. 
Also, the engine has hydraulic lifters,
so no need to adjust the valves.
The engine has direct injection,
which means the petrol is injected into 
the cylinders, and the intake valves
gradually get carbon buildup, especially if 
you mainly drive in city traffic. This means
that once every 30-40 thousand kilometers, the 
engine will require valve cleaning. Otherwise,
it will gradually lose power, and the 
revolutions will start jumping when idling.
Pay attention that the spark plugs will have to 
be replaced once every 30,000 kilometers. Somehow,
the plugs and coils don’t last long in 
these engines, probably because of a lot
of heat in their area. Also, if you feel 
sudden power loss, pay attention to the
turbocharger piping. It’s a very common issue 
when one of the pipes falls off and the engine
goes crazy. Fortunately, it's a quick DIY 
repair to put the pipe back in its place.
The engine will start consuming oil after about 
150,000 kilometers, and the consumption will
grow step by step. Unless it’s more than 1 
liter per 1000 kilometers, there is nothing
to worry about. But the engine has quite 
limited possibilities for repairs since it
doesn’t have iron sleeves in the block. Instead, 
it uses cylinder coating for better efficiency,
but once something is wrong with the block, the 
engine is dead. So, very high oil consumption
will tell you about the need to replace the 
engine unless there is a leak that you can find.
I wouldn’t say the engine is very cool to drive, 
especially if you love active driving. It has
a significant turbo lag and is not tuned 
for sporty driving at all. Additionally,
you shouldn’t expect magically good 
fuel consumption. It burns surprisingly
much fuel unless you barely touch the gas pedal.
Other than that, these are quite good engines that
can last up to 300 or even 350 thousand kilometers 
if maintained well. But they require high-quality
oil, and also expensive chain kit replacement, 
as well as periodic intake valve cleaning.

videos.title: 1.0 TCE engine problems in Renault and Dacia vehicles
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.0 TCE engine is the 3-cylinder turbocharged 
petrol unit used in Renault and Dacia vehicles.
It was first introduced in 2018 as the TCE 100 
H4Dt engine in the Clio and Capture. It was also
downgraded to TCE 90 later to fit into ecology 
rules. Then it was updated to the TCE 110 H5Dt
in 2020 and used in the Megane. Also, this engine 
was largely used in all Dacia models. And the same
engine was used in the Nissan Micra as the HR10DET 
with a different plastic cover and a Nissan logo,
but all technologies were the same.
When it comes to common problems,
I wouldn’t say these engines were as bad as they 
were originally expected to be. One of the common
issues is significant random punching in early 
model years between 2018 and 2020. But there was
a software update that fixed this issue. So if you 
experience a sudden loss of power, contact your
Renault dealership and have the update installed.
Also, these engines are prone to oil leaks,
especially there is a common leak in 
the valve cover seal. But fortunately,
it’s fixed with the new seal, and it’s a very 
cheap solution, so it's not a big problem here.
These engines use timing chains, and they are 
not eternal. Renault claims that the chain will
last the entire life of the engine, and they 
are not wrong, since when the chain fails,
the engine will die. But, on average, owners hear 
some minor rattling starting at 120,000 miles,
so it makes sense to replace the chain kit 
in these engines at 100,000 miles or 160,000
kilometers to avoid chain jumping or braking. 
It’s quite unpleasant that the phaser may also
require replacement at about 120,000 miles. So, 
if you consider driving your car for a long time,
you should replace the chain kit along with 
the phaser. Also, it’s important to use OEM
oil or at least choose something with 
the needed viscosity to avoid premature
failure of the phaser and chain tensioner. The 
difference between the 100 and 110-horsepower
engines is that the more powerful one has 
two phasers, while the 100-horsepower model
and 90-horsepower model has only an intake 
phaser, which makes it cheaper to service.
Also, the 100-horsepower model has no hydraulic 
lifters, while the more powerful version is
equipped with them. So, if you own the H4Dt model, 
you may need to adjust the valve clearance once
every 60-80 thousand miles. But the procedure 
is only needed when the engine runs roughly and
vibrates or loses power. If it works flawlessly, 
there is no need to invest in valve adjustment.
Also, one more significant difference between the 
two versions of the 1.0 TCE is the fuel injection
system. The 100-horsepower version has port 
injectors that are reliable and don’t usually
cause problems. The 110-horsepower engine has 
direct injection and suffers from intake valve
contamination. This is not a serious problem, but 
just a feature of all direct injection engines
that are used in city traffic and rarely 
run at high revolutions. Sooner or later,
the intake valves will get clogged, and this 
will affect the power and stability of the
engine's work. Fortunately, valve cleaning in 
a good garage is not an expensive service now.
Other than that, I don’t see a lot of problems 
with these engines. For their size and price,
they are quite good machines that have extremely 
low fuel consumption and are good for city driving
with good torque. You will feel a lack of power 
when trying to overtake someone on a highway,
but other than that, the engine 
doesn’t feel extremely underpowered.
Turbochargers sometimes have problems with 
wastegates getting stuck, and you feel a
loss of power and rough running, as well as 
get warnings and lights on the dashboard.
Fortunately, the engine has quite a simple 
turbocharger that is cheap and easy to repair.
I’ve seen some reports for excessive oil 
consumption, but I’m not sure if it’s very
common for these engines. They will certainly 
burn some oil, but as long as it’s less than
half a liter per 1000 miles, it should 
be fine and won’t cause any problems.
So, I don’t think the 1.0 TCE is a bad choice. The 
110-horsepower version seems to be a little more
modern in terms of technologies, but it also 
fails earlier since it powers larger vehicles
like the Megane, and gets a lot of wear and 
tear because of this. The TCE 90 and TCE 100
seem to be solid engines with affordable 
service costs, very good fuel economy,
and they don’t feel extremely underpowered. But, 
of course, like any modern engine, they need
extremely good maintenance to last long enough. 
And I believe 250,000 kilometers or 170,000 miles
is a good average lifespan that you should keep 
in mind if you own a car with such an engine.

videos.title: GM 1.2L Turbo engine (LIH, LBP): Problems and life expectancy
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.2-liter 3-cylinder turbo engine 
is mainly used in the Buick Encore,
and also Chevy Trailblazer and Chevy Trax in 
the US. There are versions named LIH and LBP
and the only difference is that the LBP model is 
flex-fuel, so it can burn ethanol-based fuel with
no consequences. These engines are turbocharged 
and they offer pretty good power of 137 horsepower
and also impressive torque at 167 pound-feet.
But you are probably more interested in the
common issues with these engines. And since 
they have been made since 2019, we already know
a lot about their behavior after they reach 
100,000 miles or more, so there is a pretty
obvious understanding of the common problems.
First of all, I should point out that these
engines have a so-called wet timing belt. This 
is the belt that’s moved inside the engine and
works the same way as a chain would work. But it 
created less noise. And the problem with these
belts is that after about 50,000 miles, they start 
degrading and contaminating oil with their debris.
If such a belt is not replaced on time, it will 
clog the oil filter and eventually clog the oil
pump. When you see the oil pressure warning light 
on the dash of your Chevy or Buick equipped with
this engine, it’s most likely that the problem 
is huge and driving further is not a good idea.
The engine needs to be cleaned properly, 
otherwise you can kill it any minute. So,
I believe if you replace the belt here once 
every 40,000 miles, you’ll be good to go. Also,
the oil should only be used OEM because it affects 
the belt and any aftermarket oil may speed up the
process of belt degrading. Unfortunately, GM 
makes the same mistake as Ford and Citroen
with their wet-belt engine and recommends belt 
replacement at 150,000 miles. Well, I don’t think
a single 1.2 turbo engine will survive 150K miles 
without belt replacement. So keep an eye on it.
Other than that, these engines only have minor 
issues. They are pretty noisy and they vibrate
a little more than you would expect. Also, these 
engines have an overengineered start-stop system
that you will want to turn off every time you 
start your vehicle. And I’ve heard a lot of
complaints about the EVAP system throwing various 
warning lights and codes. But usually, those will
go away after some time causing no real harm.
One more important thing is that you shouldn’t
expect a lot of miles from this engine. I believe 
150,000 miles should be the average lifespan of
the 1.2-liter turbo since the engine only has 
3 cylinders and works with serious vibrations
all the time. After 100,000 miles, it will start 
consuming a little oil and at about 150,000 miles,
the engine may not be wise to repair since 
it’s about to end its short and bright life.

videos.transcript_text:
hi I'm Robin and I'm about to change the
turbo in this car but before I do I want
to explain to you how to quickly spot if
your turbo is malfunctioning
[Music]
[Applause]
[Music]
the turbo gives power to your engine and
makes driving and accelerating more
exciting but it can also fail and in the
worst case scenario your engine can stop
now some of the early signs of damage
aren't very consequential but they're
easy to recognize left unchecked these
can become worse over time and cause
catastrophic damage now let's review
some of the most common symptoms to see
if your turbo has broken down or is
about to break down here's what you can
experience lack of power now if you know
your car or if you have experienced
driving turbocharged cars this one can
be difficult to overlook the engine
doesn't produce the power output as it
should it's just not as perky as it used
to be you can also feel a kind of lack
of momentary engine response when you
want to accelerate sometimes the engine
won't even get to a higher revs level
and the turbo lag seems to be much
longer than usual now this all may refer
to an under boost condition where the
turbo suffers from some severe failure
or where the system can't deliver the
boost to the engine
[Music]
now let's talk about smoking exhaust a
healthy engine should never emit any
visible smoke from the exhaust system
now there are many factors that can
cause an engine to emit smoke but a
failing turbo is one of them the
following smoke colors apply universally
to both gasoline and diesel engines
bluish white smoke is a sign the engine
is burning oil now this is a real
problem because oil should never be a
part of the combustion process high
engine wear or crankcase ventilation
system malfunction are usually the root
of the problem here the most common
turbo related issue is leaky shaft seals
now white smoke can indicate that the
engines burning coolant there's moisture
present in the intake or you have high
EGR rates in terms of the turbo league
coolant burning symptoms may occur
because of leaks in water-cooled turbo
models
black smoke refers to an incomplete
combustion now this just means that the
fuel that's getting into the engine
isn't burning completely a lot of things
can cause this but the main one is a
blockage in the proper oxygen supply a
broken turbo is a real issue especially
if we can't deliver proper air to the
engine broken elements like a failing
compressor wheel seizures or impaired
boost control are all issues related to
black smoke another issue could be leaks
within the ducts that deliver the charge
air or an intercooler that may not be
sealed or suffer from inner clogs or
even surface perforation noises can be
an obvious symptom of severe
turbocharger failure you can't miss them
because they amplify as the engine revs
up and sometimes you can even hear them
loudly inside the cabin a whining or
siren noise is a very distinctive turbo
failure sign and indicates that there's
a failure with the turbo on the
compressor side whether it's a shaft
with too much play or that's out of
balance or bent or chipped compressor
blades they'll all result in Visnu's
until the turbo completely collapses
whistling noises are common for leaks
within the charged air ducts
whereas hissing noises are usually
accompanied by an exhaust spell in the
cabin and are related to leaks on the
exhaust side of the turbo this is what a
hissing sound sounds like
[Music]
and the last possible symptom caused by
turbo failures are errors registered by
the engine control unit or the ECU and
the illuminated check engine light on
the dashboard is pretty common but
you'll register specific error codes via
obd diagnostics in some circumstances
the malfunctioning turbo can result in
the engine being put into limp mode with
reduced revs and power but this isn't a
fixed rule and some of the most
catastrophic turbo failures can happen
without any of the error codes mentioned
so these error codes can typically refer
to lack of proper boost pressure turbo
boost control device failures or erratic
readings from the MAF or ma P sensor now
if some of these symptoms are present
don't panic it could be that the turbo
is broken but a thorough system check
has to be performed to confirm it before
replacing the part you have to find out
what the problem is and repair it in the
following episodes we'll talk about
common turbocharger failures talk about
some of their root causes and discuss
some installation and troubleshooting
tips I'm Robin thanks for letting me
show you what's under the hood hey guys

Vauxhall 1.2 Turbo engine: Problems and key features
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.2-liter turbo engine in Vauxhall and Opel 
cars is actually the Peugeot EB2DTS engine.
Exactly the same engine is used in the Opel and 
Vauxhall Corsa F, Opel and Vauxhall Grandland X,
and also Peugeot 208, Peugeot 308, and Citroen C4. 
The slightly different variations of this engine
are also used in tons of other European cars 
that have connections with the Peugeot-Citroen
group. So, they are very popular and there are 
a lot of these engines on the road. By the way,
the engine was engineered back 
in 2014, so it’s not that fresh.
So, this is the 1.2-liter 3-cylinder 
turbocharged engine with direct injection,
the belt-driven timing system, and additional 
balance shafts in the block. The timing belt
is wet which means it’s located inside the engine 
and is submerged in oil bath. I will cover this a
little later in the problems section. The engine 
has a dual VTi valve timing system for efficiency
and economy. One more interesting thing 
is that the engine doesn’t have valve
lifters and you will have to adjust the 
valve clearance once every several years.
Interestingly, even in the Grandland X, 
the engine shows a pretty good dynamic
with its 130 horsepower. But the power is less 
important than torque which is pretty high here
at 240 Newton meters. Also, the engines are 
known for extremely good fuel economy. The
average combined city-highway consumption is 5.5 
liters per 100 kilometers or 51 MPG UK. Well,
it’s close to impossible to achieve these 
claimed figures in real life, but still,
it’s very impressive for an SUV.
So, when it comes to lifespan,
these engines are claimed to last about 250,000 
kilometers till you have first expensive repairs.
This is an average estimated lifespan, so 
some will drive these engines longer while
others may replace them at a lower mileage.
Opel and Vauxhall started using this engine in
2017, so they avoided having a bunch of 
initial problems. Earlier engine models
had issues with blocks and crankshafts 
but Peugeot fixed them pretty quickly.
One of the problems is the carbon buildup 
on intake valves because this is the direct
injection engine and fuel doesn’t travel 
through the valves, it’s directly injected
into the cylinders. Usually, the vehicles 
that are used mainly in city traffic have
carbon buildup issues after 50-60 thousand 
kilometers and require professional cleaning.
One more issue is the oil consumption that starts 
bothering owners at about 100,000 kilometers.
This means that oil rings on the pistons and 
valve seals start leaking a little oil into the
combustion chambers. While this is a relatively 
serious problem, there is nothing you can do to
prevent it. And fixing this issue will cost you 
a fortune, so owners usually keep adding oil and
driving further. You should keep an eye on the 
oil level because these engines won’t last even
a single day with critically low oil pressure.
But the worst issue is the wet-belt construction.
This is probably the worst timing system in 
the world of internal combustion engines. The
belt is pretty hard to replace that’s why labor 
costs are insane. The manufacturer says it will
last 180,000 kilometers. But it doesn’t last 
that much. While the belt most likely won’t
break and destroy the engine, it will start 
falling apart and contaminating your oil. The
parts of the belt material will travel to 
the filter and when the filter is clogged,
they will also be accumulated in the oil pump. At 
180,000 kilometers, when it’s time to change the
belt, it’s usually too late and the engine already 
suffers from poor oil pressure. You can avoid this
and I strongly recommend replacing the entire belt 
kit and cleaning the oil pump at about 100,000
kilometers or 6 years whatever comes first. And 
of course, you should only use the OEM kits.
They aren’t that expensive but the labor will be 
expensive, so there is no reason to save several
euros on the belt and compromise quality.
Overall, this is a well-engineered engine
with only one very serious problem with 
the wet timing belt. Other than that,
it’s pretty good to drive, very economical, and 
also relatively cheap to maintain and repair.

hey everyone Brian here from honest
mechanic today's topic is turbochargers
those Nifty devices that boost your
engine's power so what exactly is a
Turbocharger you may ask well it's a bit
of engineering magic that uses the power
of your engine's exhaust gases these
gases are funneled to spin a turbine and
this spinning turbine then Powers a
compressor now here's where the fund
begins this compressor forces more air
into your engine more air means more
oxygen and more oxygen means that more
fuel can be burned each tiny explosion
in your engine becomes that much more
powerful giving your vehicle an extra
pep in its step so to speak in essence a
Turbocharger is like a personal trainer
for your car's engine pushing it to
perform at its peak but remember just
like any mechanical device turbochargers
can wear out over time due to a variety
of factors turbochargers can fail for
several reasons often related to
maintenance and oper operation let's
break them down first inadequate
lubrication regular engine oil changes
are vital if neglected the oil can
thicken and gum up clogging the turbo's
return line and preventing proper oil
circulation this can lead to leaks and
serious damage over time second over
speeding pushing the engine to rev
beyond the redline rpm can cause the
turbo to spin faster than it's designed
to which can over boost the engine and
lead to oil starvation inside the turbo
third oil starvation if oil supply pipes
are blocked or leaking or if the turbo
isn't properly primed on fitting oil may
not reach the turbo causing extensive
damage fourth oil contamination dirty or
contaminated oil can harm internal
components leading to premature wear and
tear lastly foreign object damage turbos
spin at over a 100,000 RPM any debris
like dust or metal can severely damage
the turbo wheels and Blades these are
the main culprits behind turbocharger
failure so it's crucial to be aware of
them and avoid these pitfalls now that
we know the causes let's move on to the
symptoms of a failing
turbocharger one of the first signs that
your turbocharger is in trouble is low
engine power if your car doesn't
accelerate as quickly or struggles to
reach high RPM your turbo may not be
providing the Boost it should blue
exhaust smoke is another indicator this
is caused by engine oil leaking past
worn turbo SE wheels and into the
exhaust system you might also hear an
unusual turbo whistle this high-pitch
squealing noise signals turbo bearing
wear if you notice a burning oil odor it
could be that oil is leaking into the
exhaust your car's check engine light
can also alert you to turbocharger
issues the engine's computer detects
problems through sensors and triggers
the light a drop in fuel economy is
another symptom a faulty turbo has to
work harder which can hurt your gas
mileage
and lastly look out for oil leaks around
the Turbo from worn seals these symptoms
are telltale signs of a turbocharger on
its last legs in summary common turbo
failure causes are inadequate
lubrication over revving oil starvation
contamination and foreign objects we've
walked through the ins and outs of
turbochargers how they work and the
signs that might indicate yours is on
the fritz we've underscored that low
engine power blue exhaust smoke a
distinct tur turb whistle a burning oil
odor a lit check engine light poor fuel
economy and oil leaks are all symptoms
of a potentially failing turbocharger
but remember prevention is better than
cure regular maintenance and proper
operation are the keys to a Turbocharger
longevity don't push your engine Beyond
its limits change your oil regularly
keep the turbocharger Clean and Free
from foreign objects keep an eye out for
these signs your turbo may be wearing
out if you notice any don't hesitate to
seek professional help and remember a
well-maintained Turbocharger means a
well performing vehicle stay safe and
happy driving
